course.title: Entrepreneurial Finance
course.description: Entrepreneurial finance is the money side of starting a company: how founders estimate what they need, where the cash actually goes, and whether the business can pay for itself before it runs out of money. This course walks through startup costs, runway and burn, revenue and cost structure, unit economics, the three financial statements, projections, break-even, pricing, cash flow, and simple valuation, all with plain-arithmetic worked examples you can redo by hand. Structure adapted from Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia (CC BY-SA 4.0).

questions.prompt: A startup's runway is best described as...
options: how many months the cash lasts at the current burn rate
the length of the pitch deck
questions.explanation: Runway = cash on hand divided by net monthly burn, measured in months - see 'Startup costs, runway, and burn rate'.

questions.prompt: If a company spends $50,000 a month and brings in $20,000 a month, its net monthly burn is...
questions.explanation: Net burn = cash out minus cash in = 50,000 - 20,000 = $30,000 per month.

questions.prompt: Rent on an office you pay the same every month regardless of sales is an example of a...
questions.explanation: Fixed costs stay flat as volume changes; variable costs rise with each unit sold.

questions.prompt: Customer acquisition cost (CAC) measures...
options: the average cost to win one new customer
the lifetime value of a customer
questions.explanation: CAC = total sales and marketing spend divided by the number of new customers it won.

questions.prompt: Contribution margin per unit is...
options: price minus variable cost per unit
price minus fixed cost per unit
questions.explanation: Contribution margin is what each sale contributes toward covering fixed costs, after its own variable cost.

questions.prompt: The break-even point is the sales level where...
questions.explanation: At break-even, revenue exactly covers both fixed and variable costs, so profit is zero.

questions.prompt: Which trio makes up the three core financial statements?
options: income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement
questions.explanation: The income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement together describe performance, position, and cash movement.

questions.prompt: When a founder sells new shares to an investor, existing owners experience...
questions.explanation: Issuing new shares increases the total share count, so each existing share is a smaller slice of the company - this is dilution.

lessons.title: Why finance matters for founders
lessons.grammar_note: Keep 'cash' (money actually in the bank) separate from 'profit' (revenue minus expenses on paper) - a business can be profitable and still run out of cash.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: By the end of this lesson you will be able to explain, in plain language, why a founder needs to understand the numbers even when a finance hire or an accountant is on the team. You will be able to name the single question that finance keeps answering - can this business pay for itself before it runs out of money - and describe how every other topic in this course feeds into that one question. Warm-up from the diagnostic: a company earns $20,000 a month but spends $50,000 a month. Is it in trouble, and what number tells you how long it has? Hold that thought; by the end of the next lesson you will have a name for it. Finance is not about being good at arithmetic. It is about seeing the shape of the business clearly enough to make the next decision: hire or wait, raise money or cut costs, raise the price or lower it.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Entrepreneurial finance is the study of how new and growing ventures get money, spend it, and track whether the spending is working. It differs from the finance of a large, stable company in one big way: a startup usually spends more than it earns for a while, on purpose, betting that the spending builds something worth more later. That bet only works if the founder watches the cash. The central tension is between cash and profit. Cash is the money actually in your bank account today. Profit is an accounting idea - revenue minus expenses over a period - and it can look healthy on paper while the bank balance drops, because customers pay late or you buy inventory up front. Many businesses that were profitable on paper still failed because they ran out of cash. So a founder's finance job is mostly forward-looking: estimate what you will spend, estimate what will come in, and make sure the timing lines up. The rest of this course gives you the specific tools - burn, runway, unit economics, statements, projections, break-even, pricing, cash flow, and valuation - that turn that vague worry into concrete numbers you can act on.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1: Two founders both have $120,000 in the bank. Founder A spends $10,000 a month net; Founder B spends $40,000 a month net. On paper they look equally funded, but A has 120,000 / 10,000 = 12 months of life and B has 120,000 / 40,000 = 3 months. The cash number, divided by the spend rate, changes the whole plan. Example 2: A shop sells $100,000 of goods this month but lets customers pay in 60 days. The income statement shows $100,000 of revenue and maybe a tidy profit, yet the bank account received $0 this month while rent and wages still went out. Profitable on paper, cash-negative in reality. Example 3: A founder cuts the price to win more customers and celebrates rising sales, but each sale now loses $2 after its own costs. More volume makes the hole deeper, not shallower. In each case the lesson is the same: you cannot run the business on a single headline number. You read cash, timing, and per-unit economics together.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Try these, then check the worked answers. 1) A company has $90,000 in cash and spends a net $15,000 a month. Roughly how many months can it operate? 2) A business reports $200,000 profit for the year but its bank balance fell by $30,000. Name one reason both can be true at once. 3) True or false: a profitable business can never run out of cash. 4) A founder says 'we grew revenue 50% this quarter.' What follow-up question tells you whether that growth is healthy? Worked answers: 1) 90,000 / 15,000 = 6 months. 2) Customers paid slowly, or cash went to inventory, loan repayment, or equipment - none of which reduce reported profit the same way. 3) False; timing of cash in and out can starve a profitable business. 4) Ask what it cost to get that growth and whether each new sale earns more than it costs (the unit economics) - revenue growth that loses money per unit is not healthy.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake 1: treating profit and cash as the same thing. They move on different clocks, and the bank balance is the one that keeps the lights on. Mistake 2: thinking finance is only the accountant's job. The founder makes the decisions that create the numbers - who to hire, what to charge, when to raise - so the founder has to read them. Mistake 3: chasing a single vanity number, like total sales, without asking what it cost to produce. Exit ticket: (a) In one sentence, what is the central question entrepreneurial finance keeps answering? (b) Why can a profitable company still fail? Answers: (a) Can this business pay for itself before it runs out of money? (b) Because profit is an accounting measure over a period, while cash is what is actually in the bank, and poor timing of cash in and out can empty the account even when the paper profit is positive.

lessons.title: Startup costs, runway, and burn rate
lessons.grammar_note: Gross burn is total cash spent per month; net burn subtracts cash coming in. Runway is always computed from net burn.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: After this lesson you will be able to separate one-time startup costs from recurring monthly costs, calculate gross and net burn rate, and turn a bank balance into a runway measured in months. You will also be able to say what has to change to extend runway: raise more cash, spend less, or earn more. Warm-up from the last lesson: the company earning $20,000 and spending $50,000 a month - you now have the tool to say exactly how long it survives on a given bank balance. These three numbers, startup cost, burn, and runway, are the ones an investor will ask about first, and they are the ones that tell you how much time you have to make the business work. Everything downstream, from hiring plans to fundraising timing, is built on them.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Startup costs are the money you spend to open for business before steady operations begin: incorporation and legal fees, equipment, initial inventory, a website, deposits, and early salaries. Some are one-time; others become recurring. Recurring costs are what you pay every month to keep running - rent, wages, software subscriptions, hosting. Burn rate is how fast you consume cash. Gross burn is the total cash you spend in a month. Net burn is gross burn minus the cash that comes in from customers during that month. If you spend $50,000 and collect $20,000, gross burn is $50,000 and net burn is $30,000. Runway is how long your current cash lasts at the net burn rate: runway in months = cash on hand divided by net monthly burn. A company with $300,000 and $30,000 net burn has a 10-month runway. Runway is the single most watched number at an early startup, because it is a countdown. You extend it exactly three ways: put more cash in (raise or lend), lower the burn (cut spending), or raise the cash coming in (grow revenue or collect faster).

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1: A founder lists startup costs - $2,000 incorporation, $8,000 laptops and gear, $5,000 initial inventory, $1,500 website - totaling $16,500 of one-time spend. That is separate from the monthly bills. Example 2: Monthly recurring costs are $9,000 rent, $18,000 wages, $2,000 software, $1,000 hosting, for a gross burn of $30,000. The business collects $12,000 from customers that month, so net burn = 30,000 - 12,000 = $18,000. Example 3: After paying startup costs, the bank holds $180,000. Runway = 180,000 / 18,000 = 10 months. Example 4: The founder wants 15 months of runway instead. With the same $180,000, that needs net burn of 180,000 / 15 = $12,000 a month, so they must cut $6,000 of net burn, or raise revenue by $6,000, or add cash. Example 5: If revenue climbs so that cash in rises to $30,000, net burn hits $30,000 - $30,000 = $0, and runway becomes effectively unlimited at that spending level - the business is cash break-even.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Solve, then check. 1) Gross burn is $45,000 a month and the company collects $15,000 a month. What is net burn? 2) With $240,000 in the bank and the net burn from question 1, what is the runway? 3) The founder wants to stretch that to 12 months without raising money. What must net burn drop to? 4) Classify each as one-time or recurring: legal incorporation, monthly payroll, buying a delivery van, a yearly insurance premium paid monthly. 5) If a business is at cash break-even, what is its net burn? Worked answers: 1) 45,000 - 15,000 = $30,000. 2) 240,000 / 30,000 = 8 months. 3) 240,000 / 12 = $20,000 a month, a cut of $10,000. 4) one-time (incorporation), recurring (payroll), one-time (van, though it may depreciate), recurring (the monthly insurance payment). 5) $0, because cash in equals cash out.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake 1: computing runway from gross burn instead of net burn, which understates how long you have once revenue is coming in. Mistake 2: forgetting that one-time startup costs come out of the same bank balance, so they shorten the runway the moment you pay them. Mistake 3: assuming revenue cash arrives the month a sale is made - if customers pay in 30 or 60 days, net burn in the near term is closer to gross burn. Exit ticket: (a) Write the runway formula. (b) A company has $150,000 cash and $25,000 net burn; what is its runway, and name two ways to extend it. Answers: (a) runway (months) = cash on hand / net monthly burn. (b) 150,000 / 25,000 = 6 months; extend it by cutting spending to lower burn, by growing or collecting revenue faster, or by raising more cash.

lessons.title: Revenue, cost structure, and break-even
lessons.grammar_note: Fixed costs do not change with volume; variable costs change with every unit. Break-even in units = fixed costs / contribution margin per unit.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: This lesson lets you describe where a company's money comes from (its revenue model) and where it goes (its cost structure), split costs into fixed and variable, and compute a break-even point in both units and dollars. Warm-up from the diagnostic: office rent you pay no matter how much you sell - fixed or variable? You said fixed; now you will use that split to find the sales level where the business stops losing money. Break-even is one of the most useful quick calculations a founder can do, because it converts a pile of costs into a single clear target: sell this many units, or this many dollars, and you are no longer in the red. Below it you lose money; above it you make money.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Revenue is the money earned from selling your product or service, usually price times quantity. The revenue model is how you charge: one-time sales, subscriptions, usage fees, commissions, and so on. Cost structure splits into two kinds. Fixed costs stay the same within a period no matter how many units you sell - rent, salaried staff, software. Variable costs change with each unit sold - materials, payment processing fees, shipping, hourly labor tied to output. Contribution margin per unit is price minus variable cost per unit; it is what each sale contributes toward covering the fixed costs. Once total contribution covers all fixed costs, every further sale is profit. That gives the break-even formula: break-even in units = fixed costs / contribution margin per unit. To get break-even in dollars, multiply the break-even units by the price, or divide fixed costs by the contribution margin ratio (contribution margin divided by price). Knowing your fixed costs and your per-unit margin, you can always answer the question an investor and your own nerves keep asking: how much do we have to sell just to stop losing money?

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1: A product sells for $50. Variable cost per unit (materials plus shipping plus fees) is $30. Contribution margin = 50 - 30 = $20 per unit. Fixed costs are $10,000 a month. Break-even in units = 10,000 / 20 = 500 units a month. Break-even in dollars = 500 units times $50 = $25,000 of revenue. Example 2: Check it. At 500 units, revenue = $25,000, variable cost = 500 times $30 = $15,000, fixed cost = $10,000, total cost = $25,000, profit = $0. It balances. Example 3: The founder raises the price to $55, keeping variable cost at $30. New contribution margin = $25, so break-even falls to 10,000 / 25 = 400 units - a higher price means fewer units needed to break even. Example 4: Instead the founder cuts fixed costs to $8,000 at the original $20 margin. Break-even = 8,000 / 20 = 400 units. Both levers - higher margin and lower fixed cost - pull the break-even point down.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Work these, then check. 1) Price $40, variable cost $25. What is the contribution margin per unit? 2) With fixed costs of $12,000 a month and that margin, what is break-even in units? 3) What is break-even in dollars for question 2? 4) If variable cost rises to $30 (price still $40), what happens to break-even in units? 5) Name two ways to lower a break-even point. Worked answers: 1) 40 - 25 = $15. 2) 12,000 / 15 = 800 units. 3) 800 times $40 = $32,000. 4) New margin = 40 - 30 = $10, so break-even = 12,000 / 10 = 1,200 units - it rises because each sale covers less. 5) Raise the price (or cut variable cost) to widen the contribution margin, or reduce fixed costs; either lowers the number of units needed.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake 1: dividing fixed costs by the price instead of by the contribution margin - that ignores the variable cost each unit still carries and badly understates break-even. Mistake 2: misclassifying a cost, for example treating hourly production labor as fixed when it rises with output. Mistake 3: forgetting that break-even is only a floor; covering costs is survival, not success, and you still need profit and cash. Exit ticket: (a) Write the break-even-in-units formula. (b) A business has $6,000 fixed costs, a $30 price, and $18 variable cost; find break-even in units and in dollars. Answers: (a) break-even units = fixed costs / contribution margin per unit. (b) contribution margin = 30 - 18 = $12; break-even units = 6,000 / 12 = 500; break-even dollars = 500 times $30 = $15,000.

questions.prompt: A company spends $40,000 a month and collects $16,000 a month. Its net burn is...
questions.explanation: Net burn = cash out minus cash in = 40,000 - 16,000 = $24,000.

questions.prompt: With $192,000 in the bank and a net burn of $24,000 a month, the runway is...
questions.explanation: Runway = 192,000 / 24,000 = 8 months.

questions.prompt: Materials and shipping that rise with every unit sold are...
questions.explanation: Variable costs change with volume; fixed costs stay flat within the period.

questions.prompt: A product sells for $60 with a variable cost of $40. Its contribution margin per unit is...
questions.explanation: Contribution margin = price minus variable cost = 60 - 40 = $20.

questions.prompt: With $10,000 in fixed costs and a $20 contribution margin per unit, break-even in units is...
questions.explanation: Break-even units = fixed costs / contribution margin = 10,000 / 20 = 500.

questions.prompt: Which change lowers a company's break-even point?
options: widening the contribution margin per unit
lowering the selling price with costs unchanged
questions.explanation: A wider contribution margin means each sale covers more, so fewer units are needed to break even.

lessons.title: Unit economics and pricing basics
lessons.grammar_note: LTV is the profit a customer brings over their whole relationship, not their total payments. A common health check is LTV at least 3 times CAC.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: This lesson gives you the core unit-economics toolkit: customer acquisition cost (CAC), lifetime value (LTV), contribution margin, and payback period, plus the basics of setting a price. You will be able to decide whether a business makes or loses money on each customer, and whether it can afford to grow. Warm-up from the diagnostic: CAC is the average cost to win one new customer - now you will pair it with what that customer is worth. Unit economics zoom all the way in, from the whole company to a single customer or a single sale, and ask the blunt question: does this one unit make money? If the answer is no, growing faster only loses money faster, so this is where many founders discover that their exciting revenue chart is quietly a leak.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Customer acquisition cost is total sales and marketing spend divided by the number of new customers it won: spend $10,000 to win 100 customers and CAC is $100. Lifetime value is the total profit (not revenue) a customer brings over the whole relationship. A simple estimate is the per-period contribution margin times the number of periods the customer stays. If a subscriber pays $30 a month at a $20 contribution margin and stays 24 months, LTV is roughly 20 times 24 = $480. The LTV-to-CAC ratio is a health check: a common rule of thumb is that LTV should be at least 3 times CAC, so there is room for overhead and profit. Payback period is how many periods of margin it takes to earn back the CAC: CAC divided by per-period contribution margin. Pricing sets the whole thing in motion. Three common approaches are cost-plus (add a markup to your cost), value-based (charge a share of the value the customer gains), and competitive (anchor to what rivals charge). Price is the single most powerful lever on unit economics, because a price change flows straight into the contribution margin with no new cost.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1 (CAC): a company spends $8,000 on marketing in a month and signs 160 new customers. CAC = 8,000 / 160 = $50. Example 2 (LTV): each customer pays $40 a month, variable cost per month is $15, so monthly contribution margin is $25. The average customer stays 20 months, so LTV = 25 times 20 = $500. Example 3 (ratio): LTV / CAC = 500 / 50 = 10, comfortably above the rule-of-thumb 3, so acquiring more customers is strongly worth it. Example 4 (payback): payback period = CAC / monthly margin = 50 / 25 = 2 months, meaning each customer repays their acquisition cost in two months, after which they add to cash. Example 5 (pricing lever): raise the price from $40 to $45 with variable cost still $15; margin jumps to $30, LTV becomes 30 times 20 = $600, and payback falls to 50 / 30 = about 1.7 months - a 12.5% price rise improved every unit metric at once.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Compute, then check. 1) $12,000 of marketing wins 300 customers; what is CAC? 2) A customer contributes $18 a month and stays 15 months; what is LTV? 3) Using the CAC and LTV from 1 and 2, what is the LTV/CAC ratio, and is it healthy? 4) What is the payback period for that customer? 5) If raising the price lifts monthly margin from $18 to $24 with the same 15-month life, what is the new LTV? Worked answers: 1) 12,000 / 300 = $40. 2) 18 times 15 = $270. 3) 270 / 40 = 6.75, well above 3, so healthy. 4) payback = 40 / 18 = about 2.2 months. 5) 24 times 15 = $360, up from $270, so the price rise adds $90 of value per customer.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake 1: using revenue instead of contribution margin for LTV, which overstates a customer's worth by ignoring the cost to serve them. Mistake 2: scaling spend before unit economics work - if LTV is below CAC, every new customer loses money and growth deepens the loss. Mistake 3: pricing only on cost and leaving value on the table, or cutting price to win volume without checking the contribution margin survives. Exit ticket: (a) Write the formulas for CAC and payback period. (b) A business has CAC of $60, monthly contribution margin of $20, and a 24-month customer life; find LTV, the LTV/CAC ratio, and the payback period. Answers: (a) CAC = sales and marketing spend / new customers; payback = CAC / per-period contribution margin. (b) LTV = 20 times 24 = $480; ratio = 480 / 60 = 8 (healthy); payback = 60 / 20 = 3 months.

lessons.title: The three financial statements and building projections
lessons.grammar_note: The income statement covers a period, the balance sheet is a snapshot at one date, and the cash flow statement reconciles profit to the change in cash.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: After this lesson you will be able to say what each of the three financial statements shows, how they connect, and how to build a simple forward projection from a short list of assumptions. Warm-up from the diagnostic: you matched the trio to income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement - now you will see what each one answers and why founders need all three, not just one. A projection is not a prediction that will come true; it is a structured guess that makes your assumptions visible so you and your investors can argue about the right things. Build it from a handful of clearly stated drivers, and you can stress-test the business before you spend a dollar.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The income statement (or profit and loss) covers a period and answers 'did we make a profit?' It lists revenue, subtracts the cost of goods sold to get gross profit, then subtracts operating expenses to reach operating profit, and finally net profit. The balance sheet is a snapshot at one date and answers 'what do we own and owe?' It lists assets on one side and liabilities plus equity on the other, and the two sides always balance: assets = liabilities + equity. The cash flow statement covers a period and answers 'where did the cash actually go?' It starts from profit and adjusts for non-cash items and timing to show the real change in the bank balance. The three connect: net profit from the income statement flows into equity on the balance sheet and is the starting line of the cash flow statement. A financial projection builds these forward. You state assumptions - starting customers, growth rate, price, variable cost, fixed costs, and payment timing - and let them drive the numbers month by month. Good assumptions are few, explicit, and defensible, so a reader can change one and see the whole model move.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1 (income statement): revenue $100,000, cost of goods sold $40,000, so gross profit = $60,000; operating expenses $45,000, so operating profit = $15,000. Example 2 (balance sheet): assets are $30,000 cash plus $20,000 equipment = $50,000; liabilities are a $15,000 loan; so equity = assets minus liabilities = 50,000 - 15,000 = $35,000, and 50,000 = 15,000 + 35,000 balances. Example 3 (cash versus profit): the $100,000 of revenue was billed but only $70,000 was collected this period, so despite $15,000 of operating profit the cash from customers was $30,000 lower than revenue - the cash flow statement captures that gap. Example 4 (projection): assume 200 customers now, 10% monthly growth, $30 price, $12 variable cost. Month 1 revenue = 200 times $30 = $6,000; month 2 customers = 200 times 1.10 = 220, revenue = $6,600; month 3 = 242 customers, $7,260. Contribution margin per customer is 30 - 12 = $18, so month 1 contribution = 200 times $18 = $3,600, from which fixed costs are then subtracted.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Answer, then check. 1) Revenue $80,000, cost of goods sold $30,000, operating expenses $35,000 - what is operating profit? 2) Assets $60,000, liabilities $25,000 - what is equity? 3) A company shows $10,000 profit but collected $4,000 less than it billed; what is the rough cash effect versus profit? 4) Starting at 100 customers growing 20% a month, how many customers in month 3? 5) At a $25 price, what is month-1 revenue for that base? Worked answers: 1) 80,000 - 30,000 - 35,000 = $15,000. 2) 60,000 - 25,000 = $35,000. 3) cash is about $4,000 lower than the $10,000 profit, roughly $6,000 of cash, because billed revenue was not all collected. 4) month 1 = 100, month 2 = 120, month 3 = 144. 5) 100 times $25 = $2,500.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake 1: reading only the income statement and assuming profit means money in the bank - the cash flow statement exists precisely because it often does not. Mistake 2: a balance sheet that does not balance, usually from forgetting that profit raises equity. Mistake 3: a projection stacked with optimistic assumptions and no statement of them, so no one can challenge the drivers. Keep assumptions few and labeled. Exit ticket: (a) Match each question to a statement: 'what do we own and owe?', 'did we make a profit?', 'where did the cash go?'. (b) Write the balance sheet equation. Answers: (a) balance sheet; income statement; cash flow statement. (b) assets = liabilities + equity.

items.translation: the sales level where total revenue equals total cost, so profit is zero

questions.prompt: A company spends $9,000 on marketing and wins 180 customers. Its CAC is...
questions.explanation: CAC = 9,000 / 180 = $50 per new customer.

questions.prompt: A customer contributes $20 of margin a month and stays 30 months. A simple LTV estimate is...
questions.explanation: LTV = monthly contribution margin times months = 20 times 30 = $600.

questions.prompt: If CAC is $50 and monthly contribution margin is $25, the payback period is...
questions.explanation: Payback = CAC / monthly margin = 50 / 25 = 2 months.

questions.prompt: Which equation describes the balance sheet?
questions.explanation: A balance sheet always balances: assets equal liabilities plus equity.

questions.prompt: Which statement answers 'where did the cash actually go?'
questions.explanation: The cash flow statement reconciles profit to the real change in the bank balance.

questions.prompt: A founder owns 100 of 1,000 shares (10%). After 250 new shares are issued to an investor, the founder's stake is...
questions.explanation: New total is 1,250 shares; 100 / 1,250 = 8%, so the founder was diluted from 10% to 8%.

lessons.title: Cash flow, valuation, dilution, and the metrics founders track
lessons.grammar_note: Post-money valuation = pre-money + new investment. The investor's stake = investment / post-money.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: This final reading pulls the pieces together: managing cash flow day to day, the basics of how a startup is valued, how raising money dilutes ownership, and the short list of metrics a founder actually watches. Warm-up from Checkpoint 2: issuing 250 new shares cut the founder from 10% to 8% - here you will see where that number comes from and what the company got in return. By the end you will be able to protect the cash balance, read a simple pre-money and post-money calculation, work out how much of the company an investor buys, and name the handful of key performance indicators (KPIs) that summarize the whole business at a glance.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Cash flow management is the practice of making sure money comes in at least as fast as it goes out. The common levers are collecting from customers sooner (shorter payment terms, deposits), paying suppliers later within agreed terms, keeping inventory lean, and holding a buffer for surprises. Valuation is the agreed worth of the company, which matters most when raising money. Pre-money valuation is the worth just before new money arrives; post-money valuation = pre-money + new investment. The investor's ownership = investment / post-money. Issuing new shares to that investor dilutes existing holders: the share count grows, so each old share is a smaller slice. Founders accept dilution because a smaller slice of a larger, better-funded company can be worth more than a large slice of one that ran out of cash. Finally, KPIs are the few numbers that track health over time: monthly recurring revenue or sales, growth rate, gross margin, net burn, runway, CAC, LTV and its ratio to CAC, and the churn rate (the share of customers lost each period). A founder watches these on a simple dashboard rather than drowning in every line of the accounts.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example 1 (cash timing): a business bills $60,000 in a month but collects over 60 days, while paying $45,000 of its own bills within 30 days. For a stretch it pays out faster than it takes in, so even a profitable month can drain cash; shortening customer terms to 30 days closes much of the gap. Example 2 (valuation): an investor puts in $1,000,000 at a $4,000,000 pre-money valuation. Post-money = 4,000,000 + 1,000,000 = $5,000,000. The investor's stake = 1,000,000 / 5,000,000 = 20%. Example 3 (dilution): founders held 100% before the round; after it they hold 100% - 20% = 80%. If there were 800,000 founder shares, the round issues 200,000 new shares (since 200,000 / 1,000,000 = 20%), so each founder share is now 1 of 1,000,000 rather than 1 of 800,000. Example 4 (KPI read): net burn $20,000, cash $200,000 gives a 10-month runway; LTV $500 against CAC $100 is a 5-to-1 ratio; 4% monthly churn means the average customer stays about 1 / 0.04 = 25 months. Together these say the unit economics are strong but the clock is ticking.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Solve, then check. 1) An investor puts in $500,000 at a $2,000,000 pre-money valuation. What is the post-money valuation and the investor's stake? 2) After that round, what percentage do the existing owners keep? 3) A customer base churns at 5% a month; roughly how many months does the average customer stay? 4) Name three KPIs a founder should watch weekly. 5) Give one way to improve cash flow without raising a price. Worked answers: 1) post-money = 2,000,000 + 500,000 = $2,500,000; stake = 500,000 / 2,500,000 = 20%. 2) 100% - 20% = 80%. 3) about 1 / 0.05 = 20 months. 4) any three of: net burn, runway, growth rate, gross margin, CAC, LTV/CAC, churn. 5) collect from customers sooner (deposits or shorter terms), pay suppliers later within terms, or reduce inventory held.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake 1: confusing pre-money and post-money, which throws off the ownership math - always divide the investment by the post-money number. Mistake 2: treating dilution as pure loss; the right question is whether the money raised grows the whole pie by more than it shrinks your slice. Mistake 3: watching too many metrics, or vanity ones like total signups, instead of the few that tie to cash and unit health. Mistake 4: ignoring payment timing until the account is nearly empty. Exit ticket: (a) Write the post-money and investor-stake formulas. (b) An investor invests $750,000 at a $3,000,000 pre-money valuation; find the post-money valuation and the investor's percentage. Answers: (a) post-money = pre-money + investment; investor stake = investment / post-money. (b) post-money = 3,000,000 + 750,000 = $3,750,000; stake = 750,000 / 3,750,000 = 20%.
